how: Calls recruit contributors to start, enlarge and hold national symbols.
Recruitment can discover work already underway and recur after completion reports, so a call does not establish the beginning of construction.
A joking one-line commitment answers a recruitment call without requesting a further response.
A call receives a bare written acceptance, without establishing how other readers answered or whether they placed pixels.
Participants judge available labour insufficient for maintaining a larger or second mark.
Insufficient capacity can justify maintaining the existing mark rather than moving, so shortage alone does not warrant the relocation pathway.
Participants propose and assess flag designs under pixel-resolution constraints.
A report that the first flag is finished immediately recruits work on a larger outline.
Coordinates, proposed designs and specific pixel instructions make broad building ambitions actionable.
A member proposing a proper flag receives a written commitment from another participant.
A member's proposal provides a concrete task for a recruitment call, without identifying a single starter for the entire undertaking.
A posted design remains contestable unless contributors establish consensus and change their shared strategy.
Following instructions depends on plans remaining stable enough that contributors do not waste pixels on superseded versions.
A defence-script proposal and disputed claims about automation establish discussion, not verified deployment for this flag.
The surviving script proposal and conflicting automation accounts cannot establish a transition from upkeep strain to actual machine placements.
A single room cannot test aggregate prevalence, and strategy discussion alone establishes neither formal appointment nor the absence of decided organization.
Participants explicitly prioritize holding completed-looking work and report ongoing maintenance under attack.
A participant explicitly turns an achieved position into a reason to maintain ground.
Speakers offer contrasting accounts of whether coordinated users or scripts explain canvas work.
Protection and neighbour deals are explicitly linked purposes, but this does not establish erosion as the trigger of each negotiation.
Participants ask for reciprocal peace and declare efforts to preserve the neighbouring flag.
Participants propose negotiated movement and a border intended to prevent neighbouring artwork from being overwritten.
A request for a volunteer negotiator establishes the proposed intermediary role, not that a selected envoy subsequently negotiated successfully.
A declaration of the current enemy receives a proposal to negotiate movement without bloodshed.
A reported peace decision warrants an appeal for reciprocity, but not an inference that every placer complied with it.
A participant explicitly acknowledges being unable to bind all placers while proposing a protective border.
Acknowledging limited control does not establish repudiation of a concluded treaty or a dispute over formally authorized representation.
A neighbour's request for coexistence directly elicits a border proposal qualified by inability to control every placer.
Adjacent artwork and requests against overwriting do not establish residence under another room's host jurisdiction.
Help requests meet offers conditional on available pixels and refusals grounded in existing commitments.
Requests and conditional offers cannot establish collective help arriving under strain unless available contributors actually undertake it.
A combined truce-and-aid request does not establish that a settled agreement subsequently generated help.
Resistance prompts a new-spot proposal and coordinates, but neither erasure nor completed relocation is independently established.
Invitations to join or form alliances do not establish an operating coalition or delivered mutual defence.
Alliance invitations do not establish that upkeep pressure caused coalition membership and joint defence.
Participants interpret flag conflict through pre-existing disputes about national belonging and independence.
Flag conflict becomes a vehicle for arguing language, national history and whether people can live together.
A participant explicitly treats hostility toward the flag as further reason for an existing independence stance, feeding canvas experience back into political identification.
An invasion call names a territorial rivalry and its national target in the same turn.
Participants recognize rail and bridge stories as jokes before discussing the practical subjects they invoke.
Explicitly setting the joke aside allows a prank thread to become sincere inquiry and practical explanation.
Moderators remove canvas posts and redirect contributors to the dedicated canvas subreddit.
A call for protection and expansion directly receives a moderator removal and venue redirection.
Participants explicitly cite post removals as their reason for seeking a dedicated subreddit or chat, making boundary enforcement a prompt for further venue seeking.
Ordinary corrective side-talk about grammar and time zones continues within event participation without establishing inherited group lore or a contribution to successful building.
Participants express pride in shared achievement and provincial inclusion while crediting their maintenance labour.
Completion can be provisional, with pride and celebration accompanying continued repair rather than following a permanently finished work.
Participants request museum preservation and report the final contribution and the frozen flag's damaged number.
Celebration and a museum request coexist, but the surviving statements do not establish that celebration caused preservation.
Publishing a corrected planned version establishes an alternative to the frozen result, not an observed dispute about which shared copy should be retained.
A new-canvas flag call proposes continuation without establishing subsequent uptake.
The final contribution and new-canvas call do not explicitly connect preserving the old work to beginning the next.
Participants call for converting a foreign flag and invading rival territory.
Attack calls mobilize directly for destruction without establishing that participants previously recruited for construction were diverted into it.
An attack proposal elicits a dismissive challenge to the activity's worth, not evidence that attackers were successfully restrained.
A declaration of preservation directly elicits an avowed effort to destroy the same flag, reversing the model's attack-to-restraint response direction.
Participants carry conflict through retaliation talk and post-event sarcasm about national respect.
A direct retaliation explanation supports a participant's account of escalation, not a verified collective causal trajectory from attack to rivalry.
